card.title: Choose profit play vs inventory play before setting CAC tolerance
card.summary: Black Friday has two distinct strategic modes — maximize contribution profit or clear slow inventory — and the answer materially changes how hard you push spend and how you KPI the weekend.
card.use_when: Deciding your Black Friday objective for a store with slow-moving or Grade C inventory, and setting the media team's CAC and KPI thresholds.
steps: Decide in advance which play you're running: profit play (maximize contribution profit by spending to the marginal frontier) or inventory/cash play (clear slow-moving inventory at whatever discount it takes).
Discount limits are set by margin and cash/stock — source notes you can only discount a product as much as its margin allows, and the natural candidates are Grade C inventory that hasn't moved.

If you're running an inventory play, authorize the media team to accept negative incremental contribution margin at the end of the weekend to sell through stock — otherwise they'll pull back autonomously.
If you want to do both, the source suggests a gift-with-purchase bundle with multiple tiers — it moves greasy inventory (as free gifts) while still maximizing margin on the paid products.

Understand the trade-off: the source states that straight 80% off greasy inventory is a purer inventory play than bundling it as free gifts onto good (non-discounted) products — one mode will be better than the other, depending on the goal.
Tell the media team which play is in force before the weekend, because it changes both the CAC tolerance and the KPI they're managed on.
caveats: Source is explicit that you cannot do both equally well — one play will always dominate.
The gift-with-purchase structure assumes you have inventory that's genuinely slow-moving and can be bundled without cannibalizing paid product.
Cash and margin constraints, not just strategy, determine what's feasible.

card.title: Margin math of discount depth: required ROAS grows non-linearly
card.summary: Flat discounting compresses gross margin so the ROAS needed to hold the same contribution profit increases exponentially as the discount deepens, even though units per transaction typically rise.
card.use_when: Deciding discount depth, or judging whether a proposed sale price can still fund paid acquisition
steps: Calculate pre-discount contribution profit per order: revenue minus COGS minus variable costs.
Apply the discount to revenue and re-subtract the same COGS and variable costs. Note that per-order profit falls faster than price because cost of goods does not discount.
Compute the new break-even ROAS: 1 divided by the new contribution margin percentage (contribution profit divided by revenue). Compare it with the old break-even ROAS to see the required lift.
Estimate the UPT or conversion lift the discount is expected to produce — UPT typically increases after a discount, which partially offsets the margin loss.
Recalculate target CPA at the discounted margin so the paid team is not spending against an outdated efficiency target.
Only proceed if the UPT or conversion lift can realistically cover the higher required ROAS; if not, switch to a non-discount mechanic.
caveats: The source treats discount-driven UPT lift as typical but not guaranteed; the size of the lift is an assumption you should test, not a fixed benchmark.
Verify current channel attribution and ROAS definitions in your ad platform before comparing break-even ROAS targets.

card.title: Recalculate contribution and break-even acquisition cost before discounting
card.summary: Model discounted net revenue against all variable order costs before setting acquisition targets.
card.use_when: Pricing and offer decisions — planning a promo, a bundle, a gift-with-purchase, or a clearance push, and setting the media efficiency target that promo must hit.
steps: Calculate pre-ad contribution per order as net revenue less landed product cost, fulfillment, payment fees and expected return costs, without double-counting discounts or refunds.
With $100 net revenue and $60 variable costs, contribution is $40; break-even CAC is $40 and revenue ROAS is 100/40 = 2.5.
At $70 discounted net revenue and unchanged $60 costs, contribution is $10: break-even CAC is $10 and ROAS is 70/10 = 7.
Compare a bundle or gift-with-purchase using actual basket costs and measured incremental conversion; a $4 gift does not guarantee another $100 sale.
Check clearance cash recovery separately from profitable ongoing acquisition.
caveats: Break-even here excludes fixed overhead and target profit; set a lower operating CAC ceiling.
Shipping, fees and returns can change with the offer; use store-specific assumptions.

card.summary: Model how a discount changes contribution profit and the ROAS you must hit, instead of planning discounts in isolation.

Without the curve, you will set discounts without knowing the required efficiency, and efficiency will never reach the discount threshold needed to maintain margin.

card.title: Discount rate versus contribution profit: small discounts can lose money
card.summary: Plotting contribution profit against discount rate shows small discounts often subtract margin with no UPT uplift, and required target ROAS rises exponentially near the profit-maximising point.
card.use_when: Choosing the headline discount percentage for a sale, or deciding whether a discount is viable at all.
steps: Graph discount rate (x-axis) against contribution profit per order (y-axis) using your own historical flat-discount periods.
Expect a decline at low discounts: 5–10% is not convincing enough to lift UPT, so unit price compresses with no offset and contribution profit falls.
Find the inflection where customers begin to care and UPT rises; contribution profit is a function of both average unit retail (falling with discount) and UPT (rising with it).
Locate the discount rate that maximises contribution profit per order — for the source's illustrated brand that was 20% — and headline that percentage rather than defaulting to 25% or more.

Separately model required target ROAS: it rises exponentially as discounting increases because margin compresses toward your profit target much faster than toward zero. The worked illustration put something like a 15% discount at roughly 8x required ROAS and a 25% discount at roughly 20x, which can make deep discounting outright inapplicable.
Keep UPT and efficiency data from past promos consistent enough to make this modelling possible; messy historical discounting makes it unreliable.
caveats: Both break-even and target ROAS curves need your own UPT history; generic benchmarks will mislead.
Past roughly 30–40% discounting the source considers the offer generally not worth it regardless of UPT uplift.

card.title: Model discount economics through the full waterfall before running a sale
card.summary: A 25% discount lifted AOV via higher UPT but compressed gross margin and required roughly 9x ROAS to hold the same contribution profit versus 6x at full price.
card.use_when: Deciding whether to run a flat percentage-off promotion or how deep to discount in a store.
steps: Start from the full-price waterfall: AOV $100, COGS $40 (assume all variable costs for modelling), gross margin $60, breakeven ROAS = 1 / 0.60 = 1.67, target CPA at 6x ROAS = 100/6 = $16.67, contribution profit per order = $43.33.
Now model the discount properly: price per unit falls to $75 on a 25% sale, but units per transaction rises (the source's example goes from 1.00 to 1.63), so AOV becomes $122.
Calculate COGS on the undiscounted retail value, not the discounted AOV: $162 retail × 40% = $65, so gross margin falls to $57 and breakeven ROAS rises to 2.22.
Work out the CAC needed to hold the same contribution profit: $57 - $43.33 = $13.67, which at $122 AOV equals a required ROAS of about 9x — a ~50% improvement over the 6x at full price.
Decide whether that efficiency lift is realistic for your brand using historical sale-period data, then proceed or redesign the offer.
caveats: All figures are the source's illustrative example; the UPT lift of 1.63 and the resulting 9x requirement will not hold for every brand.

The source reports some clients modelling 70-80% efficiency improvements when a rarely-discounting luxury brand goes on sale, and others modelling only ~5% because their audience is already trained to expect discounts.

card.title: Find the discount depth that maximises contribution profit
card.summary: Small discounts often reduce contribution profit because they don't lift units per transaction, and very deep discounts destroy margin faster than volume can compensate, so an optimum exists.
card.use_when: Choosing the headline discount percentage for a promo or evergreen offer.
steps: Recognise the shape of the curve: at low discount levels (roughly 5-10%), the offer is not compelling enough to lift units per transaction, so average unit retail falls with no upside and contribution profit declines.
At some point the discount becomes credible and UPT begins rising; contribution profit per order then peaks where the AOV lift from higher UPT outweighs the margin compression.
At deep discounts (past roughly 30-40%), margin compression outpaces any further UPT gains and contribution profit falls again — the source describes these as effectively not worth running.
Model your own curve by regressing historical data on units per transaction under different flat discount levels, then pick the discount where modelled contribution profit per order is highest.

Note the source's related point that required ROAS to hold a contribution target rises exponentially with discount rate, not linearly, so a step from 15% to 25% can move the required ROAS from a plausible figure to one that is never achievable.
caveats: The 5-10% and 30-40% points are illustrative from the source's graph, not measured universal thresholds; your own data determines where the inflection sits.
Modelling requires reasonably clean historical data across consistent flat-discount periods.

card.title: Calculate pre-marketing contribution using explicit delivery costs
card.summary: Separate accounting gross profit from the management contribution metric used to fund ecommerce acquisition.
card.use_when: Setting marketing budget allocation per product or category, or when a product looks profitable but the business isn't.
steps: Start from revenue excluding pass-through taxes and recorded discounts/refunds.
Subtract landed product cost, fulfillment, outbound shipping, payment fees and incremental expected return costs exactly once.
Illustration: $100 collected less $9 tax gives $91 revenue. Product $30 + inbound $4 + outbound $11 + pick/pack $4 + fees $3 + assumed return loss $15 leaves $24 contribution, or 24/91 = 26.4%.
If the $15 includes revenue refunds, remove those from the revenue denominator too; document the definition rather than mixing net and gross bases.
Use pre-ad contribution dollars to fund acquisition, overhead and target profit; calculate separately for each SKU and channel.
caveats: This is an internal contribution model, not a universal statutory COGS classification.
The source calls its full-delivery metric gross margin; preserve explicit included costs when comparing reports.

card.title: Recompute break-even ROAS after discounting compresses gross margin
card.summary: Calculate discounted contribution and break-even ROAS directly; the relationship is nonlinear rather than a universal exponential rule.
card.use_when: Choosing a Black Friday discount depth or setting the ROAS/contribution-margin target that acquisition spend is measured against during the sale.
steps: Calculate net selling price after discount and subtract actual pre-ad variable costs.
Break-even revenue ROAS = net selling price / pre-ad contribution dollars; reserve additional margin for overhead and profit.
Example: $100 price with $50 costs has $50 contribution and 2x break-even ROAS. A 40% discount gives $60 revenue, $10 contribution and 6x break-even, assuming unchanged costs.
Recalculate percentage fees, returns and shipping where they change rather than holding every cost fixed.
Keep cohort repeat-value assumptions separate from first-order economics.
caveats: The source's 2x-to-4.5x example does not follow from those simple assumptions; compute the actual store model.

card.title: Choose the discount/CAC mix that maximises total contribution margin
card.summary: Compare scenarios on total revenue and total post-marketing contribution margin, not on per-customer margin alone.
card.use_when: You are setting a promotional calendar or ad budget and deciding whether a bigger discount can be offset by higher volume.
steps: For each scenario multiply purchases × net AOV to get net sales, and purchases × COGS for total COGS.
Subtract total COGS and total ad spend from net sales to get total post-marketing contribution margin.
In the source's worked example: no discount returns $25,000; $30 off returns $36,000; $60 off returns $63,000 on the same $100,000 ad spend.
Compare this against the opposite strategy: shrinking revenue on a smaller set of customers can also maximise profit if per-customer unit economics are exceptional. There is no universal winner.
Choose the scenario with the highest total contribution margin subject to your brand and capacity constraints.
caveats: Source-specific example numbers; your conversion elasticity to discount depth may be much flatter or steeper.
Deeper discounts that attract discount-only buyers can raise future churn and erode base-price demand.

card.title: Use a Loss Leader Only With a Planned Attachment Path
card.summary: Discount a high-demand entry product near or below margin only when complementary products can reliably recover basket-level profit.
card.use_when: Choosing an acquisition product, promotion hero SKU, or discounted cart-entry item intended to increase cross-sells and average order value.
steps: Select a product with broad appeal to the target shopper. A loss leader must attract incremental traffic or conversion; discounting a weak product does not create a useful entry point.
Set the promotional price with a basket-level objective, not an item-level profit target. The source frames loss-leading as a cross-sell structure whose profit is recovered from related purchases.

Identify the complementary products that create the recovery. Merchandise them on the discounted product page, in a bundle, in-cart recommendation module, and post-add-to-cart offer where appropriate.
Make the attachment genuinely useful: accessories, replenishment items, variants, or upgrades should improve the original purchase rather than appear as arbitrary add-ons.
Use the leader in acquisition creative or comparison-shopping placements where its headline price can attract attention, while retaining margin products as the natural next choice.
Track attach rate, average order value, gross margin per order, repeat purchase behavior, and promotional traffic quality. Stop or revise the offer if shoppers buy only the discounted item.
caveats: The tactic fails when complementary products are not relevant enough to be added to the same order.
Use basket-level margin accounting; a leader can appear successful on item conversion while losing money overall.

card.title: Zero-to-One Paid Test Campaign Framework
card.summary: Run a small Meta test campaign to validate new ad creatives before committing budget.
card.use_when: You want to screen new ad creatives for a product or offer before scaling spend.
steps: Set up a dedicated test campaign spending roughly $10–$50/day, separate from your scaling campaigns.

Judge creatives in two stages: first check whether the platform allocates spend at all (algorithmic engagement signal), then check ROAS to validate that the funnel converts.
A creative that gets spend but no ROAS points to a funnel or offer problem; a creative that gets no spend points to a creative or hook problem — treat these as different diagnoses.
Promote test winners into the scaling campaign only after they pass both checks.

card.title: Meta Creative Team & Production Benchmarks by Monthly Ad Spend
card.summary: Stage-gated playbook for how many creators, concepts and new assets to run at 4–30k, 30–100k and 100k+ monthly Meta spend.
card.use_when: You're setting the creative org, output volume and budget split for your store's Meta ad program and need a scale-appropriate structure rather than copying a big brand's setup.
steps: At 4–30k/month: founders shoot the content themselves, an iPhone is fine, and you aim for a natural look. Limit yourself to three core concepts done well — the leverage is in script quality, not concept count. Allocate a high proportion to testing — roughly 60–80% of budget — because you lack the spend to scale winners yet. Use trial reels as a cheap way to validate ideas before committing production.

At 30–100k/month: bring on two to three UGC creators, direct about 25% of spend to production, expand to five to six concepts to start de-risking, and produce roughly 30–100 new creatives per month. Add a scaling campaign and begin introducing partnership (whitelisted/creator) ads.

At 100k+/month: stand up a full creative team — a scripter, an editor, four to six creators and a designer (part-time is acceptable). Commit a minimum of ~10% of ad budget to creative, run 8–10 active concepts, and produce at least 100 new assets per month (the source's rule of thumb of roughly $1k of spend per ad).
The source's framing: at 100k+ the thing you're actually buying is a system that outputs creative continuously — without it, creative becomes the permanent bottleneck.
caveats: These spend bands and ratios are the presenter's heuristics, not measured benchmarks — recalibrate against your own account.
The 100-assets figure is explicitly derived from a 'basic $1k per ad' formula, so it scales with spend rather than being a fixed target.

card.title: Seven-Day Minimum Budget Constraint to Force Creative Testing
card.summary: Set an ad-set minimum spend equal to 1x target CPA for 7 days to force the algorithm to test new creatives, then remove it to let winners scale.
card.use_when: You are launching new creative packs and need to guarantee they get a fair chance at spend rather than being starved by the algorithm.
steps: Go to the ad set (your 'pack') budget section and find ad set spending limits.
Set the daily minimum dollar value to 1x your cost-per-acquisition (CPA) target. If target CPA is $50, enter $50.
If that figure equals too large a share of your budget, cap it at 20% of the daily budget maximum.
Apply this as a 7-day minimum so new ads are tested at your target CPA; if they perform, they spend above the minimum; if not, they fade and scale down.
After 7 days, remove the minimum constraint and let the pack run freely so the best ads scale naturally.
caveats: The 7-day and 1x-CPA figures are the source's recommended heuristics, not a proven universal benchmark.
The 20% cap is the presenter's suggested safeguard for smaller budgets; verify current Ads Manager budget-limit interface before setting.

card.title: Size test budgets from target conversions, CPA, and duration
card.summary: Calculate a test's daily budget as (target conversions × expected CPA) ÷ test duration in days, choosing the conversion threshold and learning speed explicitly before launch.
card.use_when: Planning any Meta ad test (creative concept, audience, structure) and needing to know how much to spend and for how long.
steps: Answer two questions before launch: what conversion count is your statistical-significance threshold (e.g. 5, 10, 20), and over how many days do you want to learn (3, 7, 14, 30)?
Compute daily test budget = (target conversions × expected CPA) ÷ test duration in days. Example from the source: 20 target conversions × $100 CPA ÷ 14 days = ~$143/day.

Compare against Meta's standard advice of 50 conversions per 7 days: at $100 CPA that requires $714/day for a single concept adset, which the source calls unrealistic for most advertisers once you run several tests.
Because Meta's 50/7 guidance blows out test budgets, use your own commercially viable threshold instead of defaulting to platform guidance.
Decide up front what result ends the test and what action (scale, kill, or extend) follows at the threshold.
caveats: The 20-conversion, $100-CPA, 14-day example is the source's worked illustration, not a benchmark; your threshold depends on your traffic, margin, and risk tolerance.

card.title: Rotating Hooks and Angles Before Adding Media Budget
card.summary: When the offer is solid but the account is stuck, the bottleneck is breadth of hooks and angles for the product.
card.use_when: Scaling creative testing on Meta or planning a new creative sprint for a single hero SKU.
steps: Count how many distinct hooks and angles you currently run — the source says founders often stall at 3–4.
Recruit new angles from categories the product touches: use-case, occupation, gifting occasion, social proof, and objection handling.
Study outlier ads from adjacent categories for the opening frame, not just the product story (the source cites a personal-assistant gifting angle for jewelry).
Volume-test angles with consistent production sprints and kill losers quickly; expect only a fraction to print.
Feed the winning frameworks back into your production brief so new variants stay aligned with the proven promise.
caveats: Creative testing is not a substitute for a weak offer — the source treats offer as lever #1 and hooks as lever #2.

card.title: Judge creative at the adset level, not the ad level
card.summary: Meta last-click attribution makes ad-level ROAS unreliable; move KPI evaluation and budget decisions up to the adset so data has integrity.
card.use_when: Deciding which creatives to scale, pause or replicate when ad-level ROAS numbers conflict with spend.
steps: Recognize the distortion: Meta attributes by last click while optimizing across multi-click journeys, so a top-of-funnel ad warming cold audiences can show low ROAS while a follow-up ad takes the credit.
Expect reliability to decline as you move down the account: campaign-level 7-day-click ROAS correlates reasonably with acquisition; adset is less reliable; ad level is very unreliable.
Instead of debating ad-level theories (turn it off? launch it in a new adset?), bundle 5–20 creatives per adset and evaluate the adset's overall KPI.
If the adset hits KPI, scale budget without needing to know which individual ads worked — the combination works.
Use ad spend as a proxy for performance inside a winning adset: typically only a few of the ads absorb most spend, so those are the ones to model new creative on.
Build the adset as the unit of decision-making so learnings recursively feed creative design.
caveats: The source treats campaign and adset ROAS as directional proxies, not exact calculators.
Ad-level data can still inform rough creative reads via spend patterns, but the source says it should not drive budget decisions.

card.summary: The source recommends distinct formats and angles to reduce dependence on a few winners; validate with store economics.
card.use_when: Deciding whether to iterate on a single winning ad or invest in new formats, or diagnosing sudden ROAS decay after scaling.
steps: Recognize the old pattern (source labels it '2026 strategy'): find one winning ad, then produce minor variants (new background, same format) and scale. Result per the source: nearly all spend concentrates in 1-2 creatives and, when that format fatigues, the account crashes because nothing else can absorb the budget.

Adopt the newer approach: maintain 10-15 distinct formats and angles running simultaneously — e.g., three-reasons-why, before/after, try-on videos, comparison ads, ingredient breakdowns, educational breakdowns.
Inspect spend concentration as a portfolio diagnostic, then judge purchases and contribution margin; evenly distributed spend alone is not success.
Do not immediately kill a low-ROAS creative that occupies a valid funnel stage — per the source, it still has a role in moving people down the funnel.
Recheck after scale increases. In the 2026 pattern the source describes ROAS dropping as spend rose and only holding temporarily until fatigue hit.
caveats: This is one advertiser's strategic opinion (backed by claimed 2x-10x cases, not benchmarks) — test against your own account dynamics.
The 10-15 format count and the 'spend spread' success signal are source-specific heuristics, not calculation-based thresholds.
Maintaining 10-15 distinct formats is production-intensive; do not attempt without the 33% sourcing pipeline in place.

card.title: Set Test Budgets by Back-Propagating from CPA
card.summary: Size each ad set test budget as a multiple of target CPA (3x minimum, 5x preferred) so the test reaches a real yes/no decision.
card.use_when: Setting ad set budgets and kill rules for a new creative concept test in a Meta account.
steps: Take your target CPA — for example $50 per customer — and multiply by three to get the spend threshold before deciding keep or kill (here $150).
At $150 spent: three or four conversions means keep running; two conversions is a yellow light — let it run another ~$50 before deciding; zero or one means cut it.
The source personally prefers waiting to 5x target CPA (here $250) where the client permits, because the first chunk of spend is learning who to target and efficiency usually improves after that.
At 5x there is no yellow light — the decision is strictly yes or no because enough spend volume exists to judge.
Apply the same logic to ad sets, not individual ads, since concepts are what you are validating.
If you cannot afford the multiplier threshold for a concept, you do not yet have the volume to evaluate it — fix other business levers first.
caveats: This is a stated rule of thumb, not a platform mechanic; the source is deliberately more generous than the standard because early spend is exploratory.
Low-conversion-volume businesses (high AOV, few purchases) need longer windows and may still struggle to reach clean thresholds.

Treat the creative budget as a volume requirement, not a nice-to-have: sustained ad volume is what keeps fatigue from eroding performance.
Review creative output against this budget regularly to confirm production volume is actually matching the pace of fatigue.

card.title: Analyze winners with incremental attribution and a spend/ROAS threshold
card.summary: Review ad performance using incremental attribution, sort by spend, and flag high-spend ads that beat your brand's ROAS threshold as iteration candidates.
card.use_when: You are running the analysis step of a creative testing cycle and deciding which ads to iterate or scale.
steps: In the prospecting campaign, open the column set, go to Compare Attribution Settings, and select incremental attribution.
Sort the account by highest spend to lowest spend. The source notes you may instead break the view into groups by product or category depending on your business.

Identify ads that are simultaneously high-spend, above your brand's incremental ROAS threshold, and showing outsized results on that spend. The example brand required an incremental ROAS above ~1.1 for new customers; a standout ad spent $26k (over 25% of campaign spend) at 1.46.
Do not touch ads sitting right at the threshold (e.g., 1.13–1.16 in the example) — leave them for now.
Take the true standouts and feed them back into the flywheel as concepts to duplicate, vary, and iterate.
Set your threshold from your own economics — the source explicitly notes low threshold figures sound crazy but reflect what that brand can function at.
caveats: The 1.1 threshold, $26k spend, and 1.46 ROAS are one brand's example, not a benchmark to copy.
Incremental attribution differs from standard reported ROAS; compare like-for-like before judging.

card.title: Abandoned cart flow: trigger distinction and 6–8 email structure
card.summary: Build a true added-to-cart abandonment flow (not the mislabeled checkout default) with a 30-minute-to-2-hour delay and staged email angles.
card.use_when: Setting up or fixing the abandoned cart sequence for an ecommerce store in Klaviyo.
steps: Select a Klaviyo template whose trigger is 'added to cart' — the popular 'abandoned cart' template actually uses 'checkout started', so verify the trigger before building.

Add profile filters: 'checkout started 0 times', 'placed order 0 times', and 'has not been in flow for the last X days' (Klaviyo defaults to 7 days; source prefers ~14 days, adjusting for repurchase frequency).
Set the first-email delay to 30 minutes–2 hours (Klaviyo default 4 hours is described as long), and A/B test 30 minutes vs 2 hours.
Email 1: short reminder that the item is still in cart.
Email 2 (~1 day later): reviews/UGC/press — the more specific to the exact product, the better.
Email 3: objection handling — address reasons someone might hesitate to finish the purchase.
Email 4: specific USPs of the product/brand.
Email 5 (~1 day later): first discount (e.g. X% off) with 48-hour urgency, because a discount without urgency gives no reason to buy now.
Email 6 (~1 day later): 24-hour deadline reminder.
Emails 7–8 options: raise the discount, or send a plain-text founder email offering an extended 24-hour sale.
Monitor spam-complaint, unsubscribe, and open rates as you lengthen the sequence; source warns long sequences (14–20+ emails) become annoying.
caveats: Sources disagree on sequence length and suppression windows; treat 6–8 emails and 14 days as source preferences, not industry standards.
Discounts should reflect margin realities; the source explicitly ties higher discounts to margins.
Adding a post-purchase branch inside the cart flow is described as a common but not recommended pattern — the source prefers separate flows.

card.title: Set browse abandonment trigger filters and a 30-day cooldown
card.summary: Configure the viewed-product trigger with zero-order, zero-checkout, zero-add-to-cart filters and a 30-day re-entry limit.
card.use_when: Building or auditing the browse abandonment flow in your ESP so it fires only for genuinely unconverted browsers.
steps: Trigger the flow on viewed product.

Add profile filters so the email only sends if the person has placed order zero times since starting this flow, has checkout started zero times since starting this flow, and has added to cart zero times since starting this flow.
Allow re-entry after a 30-day time period to create a cooldown window.
If you run Shopify, use the Shopify added-to-cart trigger rather than the API added-to-cart trigger. The source flags this as important.

Do not split the browse abandonment flow between new and returning customers in most cases. Rationale: browse abandoners are low-intent window shoppers, and even previous buyers are re-evaluating and comparing you against alternatives.

Exception: if margins are extremely tight and you truly cannot afford an incentive for returning buyers, consider a conditional split. The source argues that for most brands doing serious volume, the incremental revenue outweighs the marginal discount cost precisely because these visitors were not high-intent to begin with.
Note the contrast with cart abandonment, where the source does recommend splitting returning customers from non-buyers because intent is higher.
caveats: Filter and trigger names differ by ESP and change over time; verify in your current account.

card.title: Abandoned cart/checkout email content: 3-stage objection sequence
card.summary: Content plan for what each abandoned cart/checkout email should contain: simple reminder, plastic-text founder check-in, then objection handling.
card.use_when: Writing the copy for abandoned cart and abandoned checkout emails before any discount is offered.
steps: Email 1 (30 min-1 hour after abandonment): simple reminder only. No discount, no overselling. Most abandonment is distraction ('phone, a thousand things going on'), not a 'no'. Include a dynamic product block and your risk reversals (guarantees, trials, free shipping, free returns). Example: 'You left something tasty behind — complete my order — why spice fans love us — complete my order.'

Email 2 (1 day later): plain-text personalized check-in from the founder. Tone should feel like a one-to-one email. Angle: 'Noticed you were checking out this product — wanted to make sure you didn't run into issues. By the way, here's why people love us.' Keep it 2-3 short paragraphs max, end with a simple CTA and a link back to their cart. This also performs well with Gmail's AI inbox prioritizing conversational email (source's 2026 claim).

Email 3 (1 day later): objection handling, not 'our brand is awesome'. Address the real frictions: is it worth the price, shipping time, what if it doesn't fit, what if it doesn't work, what if it's not as good as the photos. Frame strongest USPs/products as answers to those objections (durability/warranty for price, certifications/press for trust, clear differentiation for comparison shopping). Include a dynamic product block.

card.title: Write plain, item-first recovery copy that overcomes objections
card.summary: Recovery emails should skip fluff and let the dynamic display of the actual abandoned item carry the sale, with copy aimed only at removing uncertainty.
card.use_when: Writing copy for any abandoned cart or checkout email.
steps: Make the item the number-one feature. Showing the exact product they left behind via dynamic product sections is described as carrying ~80% of the selling, so don't bury it under graphics or long copy.
Keep copy short and to the point; the source states too many words or graphics distract the customer from completing the order.
Focus copy on overcoming objections only: quick points on shipping, product use, customer reviews, and answers to FAQs.
Use second-person, item-specific wording ('your order ships free') rather than generic broadcast copy ('all orders ship free') so it reads as addressed to them.
Answer the questions a hesitant buyer would ask (is it healthy, how long does it last, when will it arrive) with concise facts, not a blog article.
The source's stated purpose of every recovery email is narrow: remind, give the specific info needed to decide, and remove uncertainty about the buying process.

card.title: Cart/checkout abandon content sequence
card.summary: Email-by-email content plan for cart and checkout abandonment that ends with tiered offers for first-time versus returning buyers.
card.use_when: Writing the emails inside cart-abandon and checkout-abandon flows.
steps: Email 1: simple reminder of the abandoned product with a shop-now CTA and dynamic block showing the item.
Email 2: text-based nudge from the founder — informal, personal, 'you left something behind'.
Email 3: brand USPs and why to choose you over other stores the shopper is likely comparing.
Email 4: customer testimonials plus dynamic abandoned content.
Email 5: last-chance urgency — 'your order is expiring, we can't hold it much longer'.

Branch the final email: returning buyers get a founder check-in with support offer, no discount; first-time buyers get a discount opener (e.g., '15% off if you buy within 48 hours') followed by a founder 'everything okay?' discount closer.
Place the dynamic abandoned-product block at the top of every email and add cross-sell recommendations at the bottom.
caveats: The 15% / 48-hour figures are examples from the source, not calibrated thresholds for your store.
Discounting checkout abandoners can train customers to abandon deliberately — consider testing versus a no-discount branch.

card.title: Branch Abandonment Flows by Prospect vs. Existing Customer
card.summary: Split abandoned checkout and cart flows into first-time prospects (welcome offer, product highlights, objections) and returning customers (loyalty/subscription incentives).
card.use_when: Writing content and setting up conditional splits inside abandoned checkout and abandoned cart flows.
steps: Add a conditional split on 'has someone placed an order at least once over all time' — yes = existing customer, no = prospect.
For prospects: remind them of the welcome offer they're still eligible for, show their abandoned products via Klaviyo dynamic cart content, and restate why they should buy from you (USPs).

Use roughly a 20-hour delay between prospect emails as a starting point, then remind them of the offer and cart contents again and address 1–2 common objections (e.g., price, perceived value) using relevant customer reviews.
Include a minimum of three abandoned cart emails for prospects, with the third addressing another objection.
For existing customers: they are past the acquisition offer, so instead focus on other incentives — subscribe-and-save, loyalty programs, or other reasons to repurchase.
caveats: The ~20-hour delay is a starting point the source says varies by brand.
The three-email minimum is the source's stated floor, not a measured optimum.

card.title: Close with Situational Urgency and a Dropdown FAQ
card.summary: Use real, situational urgency for the final CTA and answer bottom-scroller objections in a concise dropdown FAQ.
card.use_when: Finishing a landing page or email sequence with a closing CTA and handling last objections.
steps: Use the closing block to make acting now feel like forward motion — example copy: 'you can't afford to wait... in a world driven by progress, standing still is not an option'.

Prefer situational urgency/scarcity (the source's stated best form) over generic 'act now' hype; tie it to a real circumstance the buyer recognizes, like a genuine shipping deadline or limited production run.
Place an FAQ at the very bottom in dropdown format for people who scroll straight to the end and want bare facts without being marketed to.
Write each FAQ as a question plus concise answer so scanning is easy — concise answers get read more readily.
Mirror this at the end of PDPs and cart-recovery emails: real deadline or stock condition plus short objection-handling answers.
caveats: Fake countdowns and phantom scarcity can breach platform rules and erode trust; the source favors situational urgency precisely for this reason.
The FAQ rationale that some visitors only read the end is the source's observation, not a measured behavior study.

card.title: Risk reversal and urgency placement in sequence
card.summary: Place urgency and risk reversals at the sequence point where they resolve the remaining objection, not in the first email.
card.use_when: Ordering content in welcome, browse, cart and checkout abandonment sequences.
steps: In the welcome flow, deliver the incentive first, then USPs/product education, then social proof, then urgency ('discount expiring soon') with risk reversal (30-day guarantee, shipping promise), then heavy proof, then last chance.
In browse abandon, keep email 1 as a pure reminder, put risk reversal in email 2, and put the discount in email 4 with a 48-hour framing.
In cart/checkout abandon, keep the last chance email separate from the discount branch, giving returning buyers a no-discount founder note instead.
In win-back, reserve the unique discount for email 2 and the last-chance founder note for email 3.
Use short, specific urgency ('expires in 24 hours') rather than vague pressure.
caveats: Aggressive urgency in the last email may cost list goodwill; the source recommends testing timing and tone.

card.title: Recover cart abandonment without making discounts the only answer
card.summary: Use a prompt, escalating recovery sequence that resolves shipping, returns, fit, and compatibility concerns before relying on incentives.
card.use_when: Building or auditing cart- and browse-abandonment email and SMS flows for shoppers who began but did not complete a purchase.
steps: Trigger the first recovery contact quickly after abandonment; the source recommends acting within the first hour rather than waiting until the next day.
Build a sequence across roughly 72 hours that escalates from product and objection resolution to urgency and, where justified, an incentive.
Lead with the objections most likely to block completion: total cost, delivery timing, return policy, fit, compatibility, or product suitability.
Ensure the checkout itself displays fees transparently; recovery messages cannot fully compensate for a recurring late-cost surprise.
Use reviews and credibility signals near checkout and in recovery content when trust is the likely barrier.
Use real-time intent signals where available to tailor reassurance, such as sizing help, shipping estimates, or compatibility information.
Reserve free shipping or time-limited discounts for situations where their incremental order value outweighs margin loss, and compare recovery revenue with a holdout when possible.
caveats: The source’s first-hour and 72-hour timings are a framework to test, not proven universal optima.
Frequent recovery discounts can train shoppers to abandon intentionally; evaluate net margin and future behavior, not recovered-order count alone.

card.title: Build testimonial and FAQ emails around objections

For the FAQ email, gather real questions from chat features on your site, emails to you, Facebook messages and page comments. The source says review this material for ideas if you do not already know what to include.

Open the FAQ email by acknowledging the questions, e.g. 'over the last few days I've been telling you about my product and you sent in so many great questions I wanted to address them all at once', then answer each question in turn.

card.title: Answer objections in proportion to price and complexity
card.summary: Scale PDP information density to how complex, expensive or unfamiliar the product is.
card.use_when: Deciding how much content a specific product page needs during PDP build-out.
steps: List every objection a buyer could raise: taste, sizing, durability, ethics claims, comfort, shipping, returns.
Match each objection to a proof format — reviews and user videos for subjective claims (taste, comfort), spec sheets and certifications for technical claims, comparison tables for price objections.
Back abstract claims with evidence: if you say a fabric stretches better, cite the certification; if you say the legging prevents camel toe, show women saying so or photos demonstrating it.
If positioning the brand as a new invention or as sustainable, explain why the claim is true and how the product differs, rather than just stating it.
Publish a detailed size chart for any apparel product — sizing is the biggest hesitation point in that niche.
Add fabric and care information (material benefits, washing instructions, support level for bras and leggings) so buyers don't fear the item degrading.
Rule of thumb from the source: the more complicated and the more expensive the product, the more detailed the product page should be.
caveats: Content depth is a source heuristic, not a tested threshold; a cheap, familiar product does not need a dense page.

card.title: Answer purchase-step objections beside Add to Cart and checkout
card.summary: Treat uncertainty about proceeding—delivery, returns, payment, fit, or what happens next—as a distinct CRO problem from objections to the product itself.
card.use_when: Shoppers see a clear product offer but abandon at Add to Cart, a bundle selector, a subscription choice, or checkout because the next step feels risky or unclear.
steps: Separate product objections from first-step objections. Product objections concern quality, suitability, price, or efficacy. First-step objections concern the act of moving forward: whether checkout is safe, when payment occurs, how delivery works, or whether returns are possible.
Identify the dominant uncertainty using support contacts, reviews, session recordings, checkout-abandonment feedback, and shopper interviews.

Place a plain-language answer beside the relevant action. Examples include when an order ships, whether a discount is applied automatically, how easy exchanges are, how subscription skips or cancellations work, or why a requested detail is needed to calculate delivery.

Explain the purpose of information when it is requested. If location is needed to show delivery dates or product availability, say so before asking rather than leaving shoppers to infer a more intrusive reason.
Add relevant social proof around the action where it helps make proceeding feel normal and safe, then measure completed purchases and margin rather than merely CTA clicks.
caveats: Objections differ by category and shopper segment; do not copy generic reassurance without evidence it addresses the actual hesitation.
Clear disclosure cannot compensate for genuinely unattractive shipping, return, pricing, or subscription terms.

card.title: Configure Shopify product page section settings

Hide the vendor block unless you stock multiple brands, in which case showing the brand helps buyers.
Keep the sticky add-to-cart, especially on mobile — it is user-friendly and eases navigation; you can choose position (center/left/right) and button style.
Breadcrumbs are generally recommended and can be kept for SEO.
Keep image zoom on if you have good photos, since detail viewing helps buyers.

card.title: Resolve pre-purchase objections beside product, cart and checkout actions
card.summary: Design for hesitant shoppers by answering the uncertainties that stop a first purchase before asking them to add to cart or pay.
card.use_when: A store has significant PDP or cart abandonment, especially where delivery coverage, returns, fit, subscription terms or post-purchase process are unclear.
steps: Separate product objections from first-step inertia. Product objections may concern price or features; first-step objections are the doubts that stop a shopper from adding to cart, starting checkout or entering payment details at all.

Use customer-service logs, onsite search, reviews, return reasons, session recordings and survey responses to identify unanswered questions. Common ecommerce examples include delivery area and timing, total cost, duties, stock availability, sizing, compatibility, return process, recurring-charge terms and what happens after purchase.

Answer the relevant questions immediately near the associated decision. Put fit and compatibility reassurance near variant selection; delivery and returns near add to cart; payment, fulfilment and support reassurance in cart and checkout.

Describe the post-purchase sequence concretely: order confirmation, dispatch timing, tracking, packaging expectations, subscription management and support route. This reduces uncertainty without promising fulfilment standards you cannot meet.
Focus optimisation on undecided shoppers rather than only the determined buyers who will purchase despite missing information.
Test the content’s effect on add-to-cart, checkout start, purchase completion, cancellation and return rates.
caveats: The source provides a construction-service example, not a complete ecommerce objection list; validate objections against your own shoppers.
More reassurance content can create clutter. Prioritise the questions with demonstrated frequency or commercial impact.

Generate different image sizes for different pages, usages and devices rather than one master asset for all placements.
Combine with a CDN so the correctly sized image is fetched from a server geographically near the shopper.
caveats: High-quality imagery is a conversion asset for shops, so balance compression against visible quality loss rather than maximizing compression.
Do not ship a single downsized master everywhere; the source specifically recommends per-device and per-placement variants.

card.title: Fix product pages: visuals, descriptions, trust signals and CTA
card.summary: Address the common conversion killers on product pages — weak images, generic descriptions, mismatched price-to-value, missing reviews or murky returns — with specific fixes.
card.use_when: Your biggest funnel drop is before add-to-cart, or product pages get traffic but don't convert.
steps: Visuals: add at least 3–5 real images showing multiple angles with working zoom so buyers can see texture and stitching. Consider a product video or 3D model, which Shopify supports free alongside photos. Example from the source: footwear brand Vessi uses four images per product covering all angles, one lifestyle shot in a puddle, plus a 360-degree video. For anything where size or fit matters, include a scale-reference photo.

Descriptions: lead with benefits and support with features ('so soft you'll forget you're wearing it' over 'made with organic cotton'), include sizing and fit information where relevant, and avoid generic copy with no story.
Trust: install a review app (the source names Judge.me, Loox and Yotpo) and push for user-generated photos; a murky return policy removes trust — make it clear.
Price vs perceived value: if the drop sits here, either strengthen value presentation or reconsider the price, since misalignment is one of the three named conversion killers.
CTA: make Add to cart impossible to miss with high contrast and clear text, and test a sticky add-to-cart button that stays visible as mobile shoppers scroll through description and reviews.
Consider showing inventory levels when stock is low — 'only three left' creates genuine urgency that can prompt buying now rather than bookmarking.
Ask Sidekick: 'Analyze my top product page and suggest improvements' to get recommendations based on your actual content.
caveats: The claim that product pages cause 60–70% of conversion killers is the presenter's framing, not a measured benchmark.
Low-stock urgency only works if stock levels are genuine.

Make price, shipping cost, delivery expectation, return policy, and warranty details easy to locate without forcing a shopper away from the buying task.

card.summary: Shrink product/hero images and choose JPEG/PNG/MP4 by need rather than uploading DSLR originals.
card.use_when: Speed tests show images are too large for mobile, or your store's pages load slowly because of oversized image assets.
steps: Convert large source images to a full-HD-size JPEG compressed under 1 MB — the source states this is sufficient for any screen size, especially for mobile-majority traffic.
Use PNG only when the image needs a transparent background; avoid animated GIFs (unprofessional and heavy) and instead upload a compressed MP4 using an HTML video tag.
For above-the-fold assets like the first hero or main product image, do not lazy-load them; they should load immediately.
Use preload='none' on videos so they load without blocking other elements.
Apply loading='lazy' to images not initially visible; for a carousel, lazy-load the second, third (etc.) images but not the first.
caveats: 'Under 1 MB JPEG is sufficient for any screen' is the presenter's rule of thumb, not a measurement of your specific catalog.
Lazy-loading the first visible image causes layout issues and hurts speed — the source calls this out as a common mistake.

card.title: Answer four purchase questions above the fold
card.summary: Ensure the first mobile view answers what the product is, why this option, why act now, and why trust the store.
card.use_when: Auditing the mobile above-the-fold area of a PDP or paid-traffic landing page where shoppers may leave before scrolling.
steps: Review the page on a physical phone as well as desktop, because the source emphasizes that ecommerce traffic is predominantly mobile.
Make the product and its intended use immediately identifiable; do not require visitors to infer what is being sold.
State why this product is the relevant choice through a differentiator or unique mechanism.
Give a legitimate reason to purchase now, such as a clearly defined offer, availability consideration, or other substantiated purchase incentive.
Show credible trust support in the initial view where feasible, such as relevant review evidence or an outcome-focused proof element.
Fix unanswered questions before spending effort on lower-page cosmetics or minor design refinements.
caveats: The source argues that stock Shopify-style pages commonly fail these questions; assess your actual theme and page rather than assuming it does.

card.title: Use an A/B calculator to set test duration on low-traffic stores
card.summary: Low-traffic stores should calculate required sample size before testing, or make sequential changes measured with session recordings instead.
card.use_when: Planning how many tests your store can realistically run per month given its traffic and current conversion rate.
steps: Enter your current traffic level and baseline conversion rate into an online A/B testing calculator before launching a test. The calculator returns how long the test must run and how many tests are realistically possible at your volume.
If you have fewer than roughly 1,000 visitors per week, the source says you realistically cannot run one statistically valid A/B test per week. Do not call a result a win on a sample that small.

For low-traffic stores in the range of about 10,000 to 20,000 visitors per month, the source's agency instead reviews objective behavioral data (the source mentions Microsoft Clarity session recordings and heatmaps) and makes changes based on observed friction, then measures what happens over time.

With this sequential approach, accept that you cannot attribute the change to a single element the way a 50/50 split would. Treat it as directional evidence and keep the change only if the metric holds after a full business cycle.
Re-run the calculator whenever traffic or conversion baseline shifts materially, since the required sample size changes.
caveats: Statistical significance thresholds and calculator interfaces vary by tool; verify the current tool's assumptions.
Sequential before/after changes are confounded by seasonality, promotions and traffic mix; the source explicitly frames them as an alternative to, not equivalent of, a true split test.

card.title: The 25k Visitor A/B Testing Threshold
card.summary: The source warns that A/B or split testing is mathematically unreliable below roughly 25,000–30,000 monthly visitors, so smaller stores should prioritize qualitative fixes.
card.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in an A/B testing tool and program or to focus on research-driven UX fixes first.
steps: Estimate monthly visitors to the specific page or funnel you would test, not total site traffic.
If the page receives below roughly 25,000–30,000 visitors per month, treat formal A/B tests as unreliable and likely to produce inconclusive or misleading results.
Redirect effort to qualitative work in that range: Clarity session recordings, scroll and click maps, and task-based user testing (e.g. UserBrain) to find and fix obvious leaks.
Make high-confidence changes — broken elements, unclear headlines, missing proof, distracting navigation — without waiting for statistical proof, since the expected direction is clear.
Once a page has enough volume, move to controlled tests (see the FigPii card) and re-verify expected uplift.
caveats: The 25k–30k figure is the source's heuristic, not a derived calculation; actual required sample size depends on baseline conversion rate and the effect size you want to detect.
Running tests below the threshold can still be useful for spotting disasters, but not for declaring winners.

card.title: Use big swings rather than micro-tests on low-traffic stores
card.summary: When a store lacks volume for element-level tests, use research-led PDP, landing-page, offer, and pricing concepts that can create a meaningful revenue-per-visitor shift.
card.use_when: Building a CRO roadmap for a lower-traffic store that cannot reliably power button-color, small-copy, or image-swap experiments.
steps: Avoid spending the roadmap on isolated, low-impact page elements when traffic makes them slow or underpowered.
Start with evidence: inspect funnel drop-off and heatmaps, then collect survey and interview feedback to identify the shopper problem a larger redesign should solve.
Build substantial variants such as a PDP redesign, a different paid-traffic landing-page concept, a bundle page, or a materially different offer or price point.
Evaluate the change by revenue per visitor or session, since an offer or redesign can affect both purchase conversion and average order value.
Use the outcome to decide whether to retain the new concept and identify the next structural bottleneck; do not assume a dramatic result merely because the change is large.

card.title: Combine quantitative and qualitative research into test hypotheses
card.summary: Use funnel and heatmap evidence to locate shopper friction, then surveys and interviews to explain it before choosing a page or offer change.
card.use_when: Creating a prioritized CRO backlog for a PDP, cart, checkout, or paid-traffic landing page instead of redesigning from preference.
steps: Use quantitative evidence first: review funnel drop-off and heatmaps to identify where shoppers hesitate, fail to progress, or never encounter important content.
Collect qualitative evidence next through post-purchase surveys, customer interviews, or usability sessions. Ask shoppers what made them buy and what nearly stopped them.
Join the two signals into a mechanism-led hypothesis. For example, if visitors do not reach a guarantee section and respondents express risk concerns, test a more visible reassurance treatment.
Write the proposed change, affected page, audience, primary metric, and expected shopper behavior before implementation.
Prioritize hypotheses only after research is complete, so the team is not merely optimizing the easiest visible page element.
caveats: The source gives illustrative tools and examples but no sample-size or interview-protocol requirements.
A below-the-fold guarantee issue is an example, not evidence that every store should move guarantee content upward.

card.title: Require statistical power before acting on a test
card.summary: Plan the sample size and duration required to detect a meaningful ecommerce effect, and switch to larger concepts when traffic cannot support a micro-test.
card.use_when: Deciding whether a PDP, landing-page, cart, checkout, or offer test can produce an actionable result.
steps: Define the primary business metric, baseline performance, minimum effect worth detecting, and practical decision deadline before launching the experiment.
Calculate the required sample size and planned duration using an appropriate current statistical method or testing platform; do not infer adequacy from a few early conversions.
Keep the test running through the planned coverage unless there is a valid operational reason to stop, rather than reacting to one poor day.
Check that traffic allocation, tracking, and variant exposure are working as intended before interpreting results.

If the required sample is unattainable, do not pretend an underpowered micro-test is conclusive. Test a larger research-led concept, improve traffic volume, or use qualitative evidence to guide a non-experimental change.
caveats: The source requires statistical power but does not supply a power-calculation method, significance threshold, or minimum detectable effect.
A statistically detectable change may still be commercially insignificant; assess revenue and margin impact.

card.title: Run CRO tests with PXL prioritization and two-week minimums
card.summary: Landing pages are never finished, so prioritize hypotheses by impact versus effort and run single-variable tests long enough to reach significance.
card.use_when: Setting up an A/B testing roadmap for a store or deciding which page experiment to run next.
steps: Prioritize with the source's PXL framework: rank hypotheses so the highest-impact, lowest-effort tests run first.
Test one element at a time so you know which change drove the result; bundling many changes hides the cause of gains or losses.
Run each test for at least two weeks so it covers a full cycle, and confirm the result is statistically significant before acting.
Document every test, including losers, and record what you believe made it win or lose; the source says losing tests generated insights that seeded later wins.
Keep testing even when you are already above average: the source notes clients converting at 5-6% still test to squeeze more, and cites Amazon running over 12,000 experiments a year.
caveats: The two-week minimum is the source's rule of thumb; required duration depends on traffic volume and baseline conversion rate.
PXL is the source agency's own framework and is not a published standard.

card.title: PXL Prioritisation Scoring for the Test Backlog
card.summary: Score each test idea with binary or simple-ordered criteria to rank high-impact, low-effort experiments first.
card.use_when: Choosing which of a large backlog of CRO ideas to run first on an ecommerce site with limited traffic or build capacity.
steps: List every test idea in a spreadsheet with a column per criterion.

Score criteria such as: is it above the fold (1/0); is it noticeable within 5 seconds (2 if very noticeable, 0 if not); does it add or remove a significant element (2 if removing, 0 if adding something new); does it increase user motivation (1/0); is it on a high-traffic page (1/0); does it address an issue found in user testing (1/0); is it supported by heatmaps or eye-tracking (1/0); is it easy to implement (1/0).
Total the scores and run the highest-scoring tests first, since they combine this store's evidence with speed of implementation.
Keep the scoring consistent across the backlog and re-score as new data arrives.
Verify the exact criteria and weightings against the source's current template before standardising on it, as frameworks like this are often revised.
caveats: The weighting is the presenter's framework, not a validated industry standard; tailor the criteria to your constraints.
High-priority easy tests can crowd out larger structural fixes that matter more long term.

card.title: Only run A/B tests that can reach valid decisions
card.summary: Assess sample needs, contamination, multi-click exposure, and time-to-purchase before treating an A/B result as evidence.
card.use_when: Planning a landing-page, PDP, checkout, or offer test—or evaluating a claimed CRO winner from an agency or internal team.
steps: Calculate required sample size for the baseline conversion rate, minimum effect worth detecting, confidence level, and statistical power. The source illustrates that detecting a 10–20% lift at a 2.5% conversion rate can require about 1,000 conversions and roughly 40,000 sessions per variant, but calculate the actual requirement for the store.
Check whether the relevant page can get that traffic within a sensible period and before seasonality, inventory changes, or campaign shifts invalidate the comparison.
Do not inspect results daily and stop as soon as significance appears. The source warns that this practice greatly increases false positives.

Prevent contamination: campaign blasts, retention traffic, and other high-intent sources can distort landing-page tests. Where appropriate, route a controlled cold-traffic source to dedicated test pages.
Account for repeat clicks and cross-exposure. A shopper who sees more than one variant may dilute or bias a simple split-test comparison.
Use primary business metrics such as revenue or contribution per visitor alongside purchase conversion, and document exclusions and test dates.
caveats: The source's traffic figures are illustrative estimates, not a universal sample-size rule.
A/B tests are most feasible where purchase cycles are short and relevant traffic volume is high; lower-volume stores may need stronger qualitative evidence and larger, less frequent changes.

card.title: Plan A/B tests around calculated sample size, duration, randomization, and QA
card.summary: Use randomized traffic, adequate duration and calculated sample requirements before acting on an A/B-test result.
card.use_when: Launching a purchase-conversion experiment on a product page, landing page, cart, checkout, or navigation flow.
steps: Define the primary purchase metric and calculate the sample size needed from the baseline rate, minimum meaningful effect, confidence requirement, and desired power before launch.
The source commonly runs roughly 50,000–100,000 sessions depending on test location and recommends at least two weeks, preferably two to four, so weekday effects repeat.
Randomize visitors between control and variation. Use multiple variations or multivariate designs only when traffic is high enough to support them.
Distinguish statistical significance from statistical power: a result may look unlikely to be random without having enough data to be reliably repeatable or commercially meaningful.
Do not run conflicting tests on the same page area. Separate tests can run on, for example, a homepage and cart, or clearly distinct page regions.
QA each experience two or three times before launch; broken tracking, layouts, or CTAs can turn a viable variation into an apparent loser.

card.title: Storytelling That Moves Quant to Qual to Hypothesis to Test
card.summary: Sequence CRO work: quantitative diagnosis first, qualitative reasons second, then hypothesised changes validated by A/B tests.
card.use_when: Setting up a repeatable CRO operating rhythm for an ecommerce site rather than running one-off page tweaks.
steps: Start with quantitative analysis: GA4 Purchase Journey, Path Exploration, Tech Overview and Landing Pages reports to locate where and on which pages the drops happen.
Layer in behavioural tools such as Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar for heatmaps and session recordings to see precisely what users do.
Add qualitative methods to learn why: post-purchase surveys, timed mid-session surveys, small-sample user testing and review mining.
The source argues qualitative input matters most when a store has under roughly 50,000-80,000 monthly visitors, because quantitative volume alone is insufficient.
Turn findings into if-then-because hypotheses, prioritise them with a scoring framework such as PXL, and test the top items in controlled A/B experiments.
Never act on a single data source alone; the source defines true data-driven CRO as two, three or four supporting data points behind each change.
Re-run user testing after shipping changes to compare before and after.
caveats: The sequencing is the presenter's recommended process, not a proven universal order; urgent fixes may still precede the full audit.
Without enough traffic, A/B tests may not reach significance, so some changes may need to be shipped on judgement with clear rollback plans.

card.title: Split Klaviyo Attributed Revenue by New vs Returning
card.summary: Klaviyo-attributed revenue is a useful north-star but is inflated by default view-through-style settings and should be split by customer type.
card.use_when: Setting or reviewing your email/SMS retention KPIs and deciding whether to optimize campaigns for attributed revenue.
steps: Understand what Klaviyo's default attribution captures: the source describes it as 5-day open, 5-day click and says the open component functions essentially as a view-through metric that credits emails for purchases high-intent customers were going to make anyway.
Use attributed revenue as a directional north star: if it is rising, you are probably reaching converting people — but do not treat it as the definitive measure of retention success.
Split attributed revenue between new and returning customers. The source argues Klaviyo's impact on a new customer is far less incremental than on a returning customer.

Do not chase revenue-per-campaign as a primary KPI. Optimizing for it drives aggressive cadence — touching as many people as possible before they buy — which the presenters say can damage brand and customer attention.

Benchmark against the Klaviyo default settings if useful, since most users run them, but treat reported increments as needing conversion-lift or incrementality validation before you make budget calls.
caveats: Default attribution windows are platform behavior that can change; verify current Klaviyo attribution settings and options in the interface.

The source is critiquing an ad claim that '50% of revenue from Klaviyo' is a benchmark; the presenters call this meaningless as a guarantee and say the figure depends on business model (furniture vs supplements).

card.title: Configure smart sending and attribution windows
card.summary: Set the smart-sending window and choose attribution windows that match your consideration cycle, then exclude inflated data sources from reporting.
card.use_when: Initial account configuration, or when email revenue reporting looks implausibly high/low and you need defensible numbers.
steps: In Settings > Email > Sender preferences, keep Smart Sending ON with the default 16-hour window so a subscriber does not receive a campaign within 16 hours of another email. This is the source's recommended default; it is customisable per brand.
Decide on 'ignore transactional messages': the source typically leaves this unchecked for most brands, meaning a just-purchased customer can still receive a marketing campaign.

Set open/click attribution windows to reflect your consideration cycle. Klaviyo's default is 5-day open / 5-day click. The source advises shorter for impulse-purchase products and longer for long-consideration products (e.g. $10k furniture with a ~30-day decision), but says do not stray far outside the 5/5 default as a conservative anchor.
In tracking/reporting exclusions, exclude transactional messages from attribution so order confirmations do not show up as revenue-driving email.

Exclude bot clicks (email and SMS) and exclude Apple Mail Privacy Protection opens from attribution data — since iOS 15, Apple pre-opens mail, generating fake opens that would otherwise claim credit for purchases.
Save, then re-check the reporting figures so you know whether your previous baseline was inflated.
caveats: Attribution windows determine how much credit email claims; changing them changes the 30% revenue KPI and all subsequent comparisons.
Apple privacy opens still appear in open-rate metrics generally unless filtered — for engagement segments, always filter with 'Apple privacy open is false'.

card.summary: Tracking hygiene: server-side events, avoiding Shopify attribution reports, and keeping GA4 as a fallback.

steps: Ensure Conversions API (CAPI) is set up on Meta: instead of the purchase event firing only from the browser pixel, it fires on your own local server and is rerouted to Meta.

Understand the two benefits: it removes reliance on the browser, which the source describes as unreliable due to iOS, ad blockers and privacy regulation, and it improves event matching using first-party data (hashed email, phone, customer ID) so data stays privatised.
Use CAPI to pass offline conversion data, e.g. an in-store purchase linked back via email or phone to a served ad.
Verify CAPI is actually working — the source says improved tracking increases the data flowing into the platform, which improves optimisation.
Avoid making decisions from Shopify's marketing or attribution reports: the presenter says these are generally unreliable.
Treat GA4 as a redundancy layer: set it up properly (events firing, campaign segmentation correct) so that if platform tracking fails you have directional fallback data.

Do not use GA4 as your primary decision dashboard — the source states nothing in GA4 can't be obtained from Shopify or the ad platforms, as of May 2026, so check the current interface before relying on this.
Note the source's context: the brands discussed are typically doing $10–20M+ revenue, where tracking being broken would be a serious problem.
caveats: The assessment of GA4, Shopify attribution reports and CAPI capabilities is dated to May 2026 and platform interfaces change — verify current behaviour.
Server-side tracking improves match rates but does not guarantee complete attribution or measurement accuracy.

card.title: Measure scaling lift on top-line new-customer sales at the SKU level
card.summary: Validate a TOF scaling campaign against top-line revenue (ideally new-customer sales on a specific SKU) rather than accepting in-platform ROAS as the success metric.
card.use_when: Deciding whether a Meta TOF scaling campaign actually worked after a budget increase, or when total-revenue-based readouts are too noisy to reach significance in a reasonable test window.
steps: Check whether the campaign concentrates on one SKU or a small SKU set. If it does, read sales for that specific SKU before and after the scale-up instead of relying on store-wide totals.

Prefer this SKU-level readout because a whole-store test needs either a much larger budget change or a much longer duration to reach statistical relevance — narrowing to one SKU raises signal per dollar of spend.
Further narrow to new-customer sales on that SKU, since the stated objective of an Advantage+ TOF scaling campaign is acquiring new customers, not re-acquiring existing ones.
Compare in-platform reported ROAS against this Shopify-side new-customer SKU sales movement; divergence means platform attribution is overstating the campaign's acquisition contribution.
Confirm the SKU was not simultaneously promoted elsewhere (other channels, promotions, email) so the revenue movement can plausibly be attributed to the scaling change.
Recheck Shopify reporting views and any current Meta reporting fields, since both interfaces change.
caveats: The source example only notes that sales 'might have gone up' — it does not report a confirmed lift, so treat this as method, not evidence of results.
SKU-level readout works best when scaling a single SKU; for large SKU-count campaigns, isolate the SKU under test explicitly.

card.title: Balance Attribution and Profitability Metrics in Your Owned Media KPIs
card.summary: Use Klaviyo attribution as a north-star indicator but drive day-to-day decisions from profitability metrics — and avoid the two extremes.
card.use_when: Setting the reporting dashboard for your email/SMS retention program, or deciding what changes your retention team should make.
steps: Treat platform attribution metrics (account/campaign/flow attributed revenue, revenue per recipient, 30-50% revenue share from email) as an indicator only. They show whether you're reaching enough people, whether flows exist and whether cadence is sensible.

Take attribution with a grain of salt: outside studies cited by the source suggest roughly 70-80% of campaign revenue may be incremental for some accounts, but it varies heavily by brand. Bigger brands can run incrementality tests.
Balance with profitability metrics: LTGP adjusted for 90 and 365 days, mapped at 30/60/90/180/365 day cohorts, plus revenue from the top 20% of customers.

Avoid both extremes: chasing attribution alone means you optimise for looking good in dashboards; ignoring incremental repeat-revenue work in favour of pure long-term LTV means you never improve today's numbers.
Use attribution as the north star and profitability metrics as the constraint-finding tool that sets your retention targets.
caveats: The 30-50% revenue share figure is described as a soft indicator, not hard science.

card.title: Complete the Klaviyo–Shopify integration and sync settings
card.summary: Wire Shopify into Klaviyo correctly so subscriber capture, event tracking and anonymous activity all flow into one profile record.
card.use_when: Initial account setup, a re-platform migration, or auditing why checkout/pop-up subscribers and browse events are missing from Klaviyo.
steps: During signup select 'sell products online', choose Shopify as the primary platform, and enter your Shopify URL. If migrating from another platform (e.g. Mailchimp), declare your existing list size so Klaviyo can guide sending-limit warmup; if new, select that you have no contacts.
Set your sender name (brand name, or 'Founder at Brand') and sender email address. This is what appears in the inbox, so it drives open behaviour as much as the subject line.
Turn on the Shopify app embed for on-site tracking inside your Shopify theme; without it Klaviyo cannot see on-site events.
Check 'sync your Shopify email subscribers to Klaviyo' and point them into your single main email list; mirror the same for SMS subscribers into one main SMS list.
Leave 'sync profiles and custom properties from Klaviyo to Shopify' unchecked — the source sees no strong reason for most brands to push Klaviyo data back into Shopify.

In Klaviyo data settings, enable anonymous visitor tracking. By default, views and add-to-carts before an email is captured are invisible, which suppresses browse-abandonment and cart-abandonment volume. Verify the current toggle location in your account, as the UI changes.

card.title: Using Incrementality to Find the Marketing That Doesn't Work
card.summary: Applying the classic 'half my marketing doesn't work' idea through incrementality testing, with the example of turning off one paid channel and watching revenue hold.
card.use_when: Auditing paid channel overlap and spend, deciding whether Amazon and TikTok (or other paired channels) are truly incremental or just double-counting the same demand.
steps: Treat overlapping paid channels as a leakage risk. The source cites a case where turning off spend on one channel (between Amazon and TikTok) produced no change in revenue because the demand simply shifted to the other channel — meaning the spend wasn't incremental.
Frame the goal as identifying the half of marketing that doesn't work. The source explicitly calls incrementality a method for discovering that half rather than just measuring what you spent.
Design the test as a holdout or channel pause and watch total revenue, not just the paused channel's reported conversions, to see whether the demand was truly new.
Be skeptical of appearances: the source warns too many operators are 'spending to spend,' and that the overlap problem is bigger than most think.
caveats: The specific Amazon/TikTok case is a secondhand example from another podcast episode, not a controlled study reported in detail here.
Pausing spend carries risk and requires enough data and time to read; small brands may lack the volume for reliable incrementality reads.

card.title: Shift from ROAS to financial-based KPIs for scaling decisions
card.summary: The source argues winning brands move toward financial-based KPIs and incrementality testing rather than optimizing to platform ROAS.
card.use_when: You are setting the north-star metric for your store's paid media and deciding what to optimize.
steps: Identify the trap: optimizing to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business, often ROAS inflated by view-throughs, brand, and bottom-funnel capture.
Understand the consequences chain: a measurement problem drives bad decision-making loops, and brands attribute credit to the wrong funnel stage.
Move toward financial-based KPIs (e.g., new-customer profit contribution, blended CAC, incremental return) rather than platform-reported ROAS as the north star.
Add incrementality tests at larger revenue levels to validate those financial KPIs.
At any level, prioritize cleaning up in-platform reporting as the first step.
Ecommerce application: for a store deciding where to scale, base the call on new-customer profit and CAC rather than a reported ROAS that may overattribute.
